content: There is very limited clinical experience with ranitidine overdose. During premarketing clinical studies, there were eight reported cases of ranitidine overdose, either alone or in combination with other pharmacological agents. The only reported fatality associated with ranitidine overdose occurred in a non-U.S. clinical study, where it was taken in combination with amitriptyline and chlorprothixene. Based on plasma levels, the dose of ranitidine ingested was estimated to be 30–45 mg, while the plasma concentrations of amitriptyline and chlorprothixene were found to be at toxic levels. All other premarketing overdose cases involving ranitidine resulted in full recovery. Clinical signs and symptoms associated with ranitidine overdose included disorientation, drowsiness, impaired memory, and tachycardia. There were no reports of electrocardiographic (ECG) abnormalities, coma, or seizures following overdose with ranitidine alone. Management of ranitidine overdose should involve general measures typically employed in the treatment of drug overdoses. It is essential to ensure a patent airway, adequate oxygenation, and proper ventilation. Cardiac rhythm and vital signs should be closely monitored. General supportive and symptomatic care is recommended. Induction of emesis is not advised. Gastric lavage using a large-bore orogastric tube with appropriate airway protection may be considered if performed shortly after ingestion or in symptomatic patients. Administration of activated charcoal is recommended. There is no clinical experience with the use of forced diuresis, dialysis, hemoperfusion, or exchange transfusion in the management of ranitidine overdose. Additionally, no specific antidotes for ranitidine overdose are known.
